section.title: Comfort for God's People
section.sectionRationale: This chapter opens the Book of Comfort, chapters 40 to 55, turning from the Hezekiah narratives and the exile they foretold toward a sustained message of hope. God commands His messengers to comfort His people, announces a voice preparing His way, and answers Israel's despair with an unmatched vision of His own incomparable power, wisdom, and tenderness as their Creator and Shepherd.
section.thesis: To a people who feel forgotten in exile, God speaks comfort by declaring their sin pardoned, sending a herald to prepare His way, and revealing Himself as the incomparable Creator who measures the oceans in His palm and yet gently carries His lambs, so that those who wait on Him will find their strength renewed.
section.frameNote: Nine movements: the command to comfort God's people; a voice preparing the way in the wilderness; the withering of all flesh against the enduring word of God; the LORD coming as tender Shepherd; the incomparable Creator who measures the world in His hand; the folly of comparing God to an idol; God enthroned above the nations; the Holy One with no equal; and the climactic promise that those who wait on the LORD will mount up like eagles.

verses.text: “{{nacham|Comfort}}, comfort My people,” says your God.
“Speak tenderly to Jerusalem, and proclaim to her that her forced labor has been completed; her iniquity has been pardoned. For she has received from the hand of the LORD double for all her sins.”

units.label: A voice in the wilderness
units.note: prepare the way of the LORD

verses.text: A voice of one calling: “Prepare the way for the LORD in the wilderness; make a straight highway for our God in the desert.
Every valley shall be lifted up, and every mountain and hill made low; the uneven ground will become smooth, and the rugged land a plain.
And the glory of the LORD will be revealed, and all humanity together will see it. For the mouth of the LORD has spoken.”

units.label: All flesh is grass
units.note: the word of our God stands forever

verses.text: A voice says, “Cry out!” And I asked, “What should I cry out?” “All flesh is like grass, and all its glory like the flowers of the field.
The grass withers and the flowers fall when the breath of the LORD blows on them; indeed, the people are grass.
The grass withers and the flowers fall, but the word of our God stands forever.”
Go up on a high mountain, O Zion, herald of good news. Raise your voice loudly, O Jerusalem, herald of good news. Lift it up, do not be afraid! Say to the cities of Judah, “Here is your God!”
Behold, the Lord GOD comes with might, and His arm establishes His rule. His reward is with Him, and His recompense accompanies Him.
He tends His flock like a shepherd; He gathers the lambs in His arms and carries them close to His heart. He gently leads the nursing ewes.

units.label: Who has measured the waters in His hand

verses.text: Who has measured the waters in the hollow of his hand, or marked off the heavens with the span of his hand? Who has held the dust of the earth in a basket, or weighed the mountains on a scale and the hills with a balance?
Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?
Whom did He consult to enlighten Him, and who taught Him the paths of justice? Who imparted knowledge to Him and showed Him the way of understanding?
Surely the nations are like a drop in a bucket; they are considered a speck of dust on the scales; He lifts up the islands like fine dust.
Lebanon is not sufficient for fuel, nor its animals enough for a burnt offering.
All the nations are as nothing before Him; He regards them as nothingness and emptiness.

units.label: To whom will you liken God?

verses.text: To whom will you liken God? To what image will you compare Him?
To an idol that a craftsman casts and a metalworker overlays with gold and fits with silver chains?
To one bereft of an offering who chooses wood that will not rot, who seeks a skilled craftsman to set up an idol that will not topple?

units.label: He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth

verses.text: Do you not know? Have you not heard? Has it not been declared to you from the beginning? Have you not understood since the foundation of the earth?
He sits enthroned above the circle of the earth; its dwellers are like grasshoppers. He stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and spreads them out like a tent to dwell in.
He brings the princes to nothing and makes the rulers of the earth meaningless.
No sooner are they planted, no sooner are they sown, no sooner have their stems taken root in the ground, than He blows on them and they wither, and a whirlwind sweeps them away like stubble.

units.label: The Holy One has no equal

verses.text: “To whom will you liken Me, or who is My equal?” asks the {{qadosh|Holy One}}.
Lift up your eyes on high: Who created all these? He leads forth the starry host by number; He calls each one by name. Because of His great power and mighty strength, not one of them is missing.

units.label: Those who wait on the LORD
units.note: they will mount up like eagles

verses.text: Why do you say, O Jacob, and why do you assert, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God”?
Do you not know? Have you not heard? The LORD is the everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth. He will not grow tired or weary; His understanding is beyond searching out.
He gives power to the faint and increases the strength of the weak.
Even youths grow tired and weary, and young men stumble and fall.
But those who {{qavah|wait}} upon the LORD will renew their strength; they will mount up with wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary, they will walk and not faint.

nacham.gloss: To comfort, console, or bring relief, sometimes carrying the sense of a change that brings ease after grief. The double command, comfort, comfort, opens the whole second half of Isaiah with tenderness rather than further rebuke, announcing that the season of God's people receiving punishment for their sin is over and the season of consolation has begun.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart, utterly other. Isaiah's favorite title for God, the Holy One, appears here at the climax of the chapter's argument for God's incomparability: no idol, no ruler, no created thing can be likened to Him, because He alone is qadosh in being and power.

qavah.gloss: To wait, to hope, to look eagerly for, often with the sense of a rope stretched taut in expectation. Those who qavah upon the LORD are not passively idle but actively, hopefully straining toward Him, and the chapter promises that this kind of waiting is rewarded with renewed strength beyond human capacity.

basic.context: After the exile foretold in chapter 39, Isaiah's book turns a corner into pure comfort. God commands His messengers to speak tenderly to Jerusalem, announces a voice that will prepare His way, and answers a weary, doubting people with an overwhelming vision of His own incomparable greatness: He measures oceans in His palm, He knows every star by name, and yet He carries His people like a shepherd carries lambs.
basic.hermeneutics: The chapter first spoke to Judah in or facing exile, promising that their punishment was complete and comfort was coming. Its third movement, verses 3 to 5, is directly applied in all four Gospels to John the Baptist preparing the way for Jesus, showing that Isaiah's comfort ultimately arrives in a person, not merely a historical return from Babylon. The chapter's vision of God's incomparable power is meant to answer real despair, not merely to impress with poetry.
basic.originalLanguages: The chapter opens with {{nacham}}, comfort, doubled for emphasis, marking a decisive turn from judgment to tenderness. It closes by naming God the {{qadosh}}, the Holy One, utterly incomparable to any idol or ruler, and promising that those who {{qavah}}, wait or hope, upon Him will find strength beyond their own resources.
basic.typology: The voice preparing a straight highway in the wilderness for the LORD's coming, verses 3 to 5, is fulfilled in John the Baptist's ministry preparing the way for Jesus, cited in Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, and John 1:23. The tender Shepherd who gathers lambs in His arms, verse 11, anticipates Christ, the Good Shepherd, John 10:11.
basic.christ: All four Gospels apply verses 3 to 5 directly to John the Baptist, the voice crying in the wilderness who prepared the way for Jesus, the LORD whose glory would be revealed for all humanity to see, Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, John 1:23. The Shepherd of verse 11, who carries lambs close to His heart, is the same Shepherd Jesus names Himself in John 10:11, laying down His life for the sheep. The everlasting, never-weary Creator of verse 28 is revealed in John 1:1-3 as the Word who became flesh.
basic.god: God comforts His people not by minimizing what they have suffered but by revealing who He truly is: the Creator whose power dwarfs every nation and every idol, and yet the Shepherd whose tenderness carries the weakest lamb. He never grows weary and His understanding cannot be exhausted, so those who wait on Him, however exhausted themselves, will find strength that is not their own.
basic.crossReferences: Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, and John 1:23 all apply verses 3 to 5 to John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ. John 10:11 identifies Jesus as the Good Shepherd. Psalm 103:15-16 echoes the image of human life as grass that withers. Habakkuk 3:19 shares the imagery of strength like a deer on the heights.
basic.oneStory: This chapter turns the whole story of Isaiah, and in a sense the whole Bible, from judgment toward comfort: a weary, exiled people are told their punishment is complete and their God is coming. That coming is fulfilled when John the Baptist prepares the way and Jesus Himself arrives as the incomparable Creator and tender Shepherd, in whom weary people find their strength renewed.

context.literary:
After four chapters of prose about Hezekiah, the book breaks into poetry, and it does so with voices rather than a speaker. The first command is plural, 'Comfort, comfort My people,' addressed to messengers who are never named. Then 'a voice of one calling' speaks in verse 3, and 'a voice says, "Cry out!"' in verse 6, and the prophet himself finally enters with a hesitant question: 'What should I cry out?' The effect resembles the throne room of Isaiah 6, where heavenly voices call and the prophet is drawn into the conversation. Many readers hear a heavenly council here as well, though the text does not say so.

The chapter moves by argument as much as by image. Verses 1 to 11 are announcement: pardon, a road, a word that stands, a herald, a coming King who is also a Shepherd. Verses 12 to 26 are a long run of questions that no human can answer, each one a rhetorical push toward the same conclusion, that there is nothing to compare to the LORD. Verses 27 to 31 then reveal why the questions were asked. Israel has said, 'My way is hidden from the LORD,' and the whole magnificent middle of the chapter has been the reply to that sentence.

Two frames hold it together. The grass of verses 6 to 8 returns in verse 24, where princes and rulers are planted, sown and then withered by the same breath. And 'Do you not know? Have you not heard?' opens verse 21 and again verse 28, bracketing the argument in a way that turns the second occurrence into a verdict. The 'to whom will you liken' questions of verses 18 and 25 are the pivots, one addressed to the nations' gods and the other spoken by the Holy One Himself.

The movement of the whole is from the large to the small and back. The God who weighs mountains in verse 12 gathers lambs in verse 11 and gives power to the faint in verse 29. Size and tenderness are made to belong to one person.
context.historical:
The chapter is addressed to a people who have lost nearly everything that proved God was with them: a king, a city, a temple, and a land. Chapter 39 ended with Babylon on the horizon, and the voice that follows speaks as though the exile has already happened. Readers have long divided over how that works. Many hold that Isaiah son of Amoz, who has just been named in chapter 39, was given sight of the future and spoke to the exiles ahead of time, as the naming of Cyrus in Isaiah 44:28 and 45:1 suggests. Many scholars place the writing of chapters 40 to 55 among the exiles themselves. Either way, the text addresses the exiles' situation, and the first readers who needed it were in Babylon.

Their problem was twofold. One part was guilt: Leviticus 26 had said that if Israel broke the covenant the land would lie desolate and enjoy its sabbaths while Israel was in the land of its enemies, Leviticus 26:34 and 41 to 43. The exile looked like the final act of that warning. The other was a crisis of belief. Babylon had its gods paraded in procession, 'Bel crouches; Nebo cowers,' Isaiah 46:1, and its astrologers, 'who observe the stars,' Isaiah 47:13. Israel's defeat could look like their defeat, as though Marduk had beaten the LORD.

That explains much of the chapter's argument. When verse 26 says 'Lift up your eyes on high: Who created all these?' it points to the very stars that Babylon's wise men read as gods. When verses 19 and 20 describe a craftsman who casts an idol, overlays it with gold and sets it up so that it will not topple, they describe the visible religion of the people around the exiles. The poor man who chooses wood that will not rot is a picture of the lengths to which anyone will go to have a god that stays where it is put.

The imagery of the road in verses 3 to 5 draws on Israel's own memory of the exodus, where God led His people through the wilderness. The exiles are being told that another journey is coming.
context.canonical:
This chapter is the front door of the second half of Isaiah, and the comfort it announces is taken up again and again: 'I, even I, am He who comforts you,' Isaiah 51:12; 'As a mother comforts her son, so will I comfort you,' Isaiah 66:13. The people's response is to sing: 'the LORD has comforted His people; He has redeemed Jerusalem,' Isaiah 52:9. The highway of verses 3 to 5 is cleared in Isaiah 57:14 and 62:10, and its destination is the road of Isaiah 35:8 to 10, where 'the redeemed will walk' and 'enter Zion with singing.'

The reversal of Leviticus 26 is also here. The exile that was announced as the cost of broken covenant is declared paid in verse 2, and the God who threatened to remove His people also promised that He would remember His covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, Leviticus 26:42.

The chapter's New Testament life is richer still. All four Gospels use verses 3 to 5 to introduce John the Baptist, and Luke alone carries the quotation down through the valleys and mountains to 'all humanity will see God's salvation,' Luke 3:4 to 6. Mark gives the quotation as Scripture's opening note on the gospel itself, Mark 1:1 to 3, joined with Malachi 3:1. Simeon is described as 'waiting for the consolation of Israel,' Luke 2:25, and Paul calls God 'the God of all comfort,' 2 Corinthians 1:3 and 4. Peter takes the grass and the word of verses 6 to 8 and says, 'this is the word that was proclaimed to you,' 1 Peter 1:24 and 25. Paul takes verse 13, 'Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD, or informed Him as His counselor?', to close his great doxology about the unsearchable wisdom of God, Romans 11:33 to 35, and again in 1 Corinthians 2:16.

The shepherd of verse 11 is a thread through the whole Bible, from Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34 to John 10, and the God who 'counts the number of the stars' appears again in Psalm 147:3 to 5, where the same God binds the brokenhearted and names the stars.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The chapter is written to answer one sentence. Israel has said, 'My way is hidden from the LORD, and my claim is ignored by my God,' verse 27. That is not mere sadness; it is a charge. It says that the covenant God has either not noticed their plight or does not care about justice. The author does not reply with an assurance that God cares. He replies with a long demonstration of who God is, and then returns to the people's own sentence and answers it in verses 28 to 31.

The author wanted the first hearers to do three things. First, to believe that the exile was not the end of the story: their guilt had been dealt with and a road home was being prepared. Second, to stop measuring God by the gods of Babylon, for the questions of verses 12 to 26 are impossible to answer with any name but the LORD. Third, to wait, which here means to put their weight on Him actively and with hope.

The author also wanted them to see that comfort and power belong together. People could easily suppose that a God great enough to weigh the mountains is too great to bother about a handful of weary exiles. The shepherd of verse 11 and the creator of verse 12 are the same speaker, and the first hearers were meant to find the second a reason to trust the first.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter describes the promise of comfort for a particular people and a particular crisis, and it describes what God is like. It does not promise that every weary believer will feel renewed on demand. 'They will mount up with wings like eagles' is a poem about what God does for those who wait; it is not a formula for a good week.

The imperative in the chapter is small and clear: comfort my people, prepare the way, lift up your voice, lift up your eyes, do not say that your way is hidden. These are commands for the herald and for the people, and they are exercised by hearing and trusting.

Verses 6 to 8 do not say that human beings are worthless. They say that human strength, glory and rulers are as transient as grass, and that God's word is not. That is why the New Testament can use the verses to call believers to hold fast to the word proclaimed to them. It is also why the chapter does not mock the weakness of its audience: it describes even 'youths' growing tired in verse 30, so the weariness it addresses is common to everyone.

The chapter also does not prescribe how long the waiting will be. The word 'wait' in verse 31 has no timeline. The comfort it offers is the presence and character of God while the answer is on its way.

debates.question: What does 'double for all her sins' mean in verse 2?

views.label: Full measure, a debt paid in full
views.case: The Hebrew word is kiflayim, from a root for folding something over. It can describe full measure, the way a double cloak is a whole one. The point is that Jerusalem's account is closed. On this reading God is not saying that she suffered twice what she deserved, but that she has been given the full sum, and that the sentence of Leviticus 26 has run its course.

views.label: Literally twice what was due
views.case: Some readers take the phrase at face value, as a sign of how thoroughly God had dealt with the sin. Jeremiah 16:18 speaks of repaying 'double their iniquity,' and the idea of a doubled sentence is not foreign to the prophets. On this view the severity of the exile is part of what makes its end believable.

debates.bearing: Both views agree on the main claim: the period of punishment is over. If one worries about justice, Isaiah himself answers with Isaiah 53, where the penalty is borne by another, and the New Testament sees the final payment in Christ, Colossians 2:14. The verse is not an accounting of divine excess but an announcement that the debt is finished.

debates.question: Is the voice 'in the wilderness', or is it the way that is to be prepared 'in the wilderness'?

views.label: A voice calling in the wilderness
views.case: The Greek translation of Isaiah and all four Gospels put the wilderness with the voice, 'A voice of one calling in the wilderness,' Matthew 3:3. This fits John the Baptist, who came 'preaching in the wilderness of Judea.' The BSB footnote notes this reading.

views.label: Prepare the way 'in the wilderness'
views.case: The Hebrew poetry places the pause after 'calling,' and the parallel line, 'make a straight highway for our God in the desert,' puts the desert with the road. On this reading the wilderness is where the highway is built, which suits the exile's return journey across the desert. The community at Qumran by the Dead Sea understood Isaiah 40:3 as a call to go into the wilderness and prepare the way.

debates.bearing: The Gospel writers were using a reading that already existed and that suited the setting of John's ministry. Both readings make the same theological point: the highway is for 'the LORD,' for 'our God.' The coming that Isaiah describes is the coming of God Himself.

debates.question: Is Zion the herald, or is the herald sent to Zion, in verse 9?

views.label: Zion and Jerusalem are the heralds
views.case: The Hebrew for 'herald of good news' is feminine, and it is attached to Zion and Jerusalem. On this reading the city herself is called up a high mountain to announce to the towns of Judah, 'Here is your God!' The rescued people are those who proclaim.

views.label: The herald is one who brings good news to Zion
views.case: The BSB footnote gives another reading: 'O herald of good news to Zion, go up on a high mountain.' This agrees with Isaiah 52:7, where the messenger on the mountains says to Zion, 'Your God reigns!' On this reading someone else announces the news to the city.

debates.bearing: Both readings fit the book, and the difference is whether the city is the receiver or the sender of the news. Both agree on the message, 'Here is your God!', and that is the point. The New Testament joins both: those who receive the gospel become those who carry it, Romans 10:15.

study.originalLanguages:
The Hebrew behind this chapter has a number of small words worth knowing.

In verse 2, 'Speak tenderly to Jerusalem' is literally 'speak to the heart of Jerusalem.' It is the idiom of winning someone over with kindness: Shechem 'spoke to her tenderly,' Genesis 34:3, and Ruth says Boaz has 'spoken kindly' to her, Ruth 2:13. The messengers are to address Jerusalem's heart, not her case. Later in the same verse, her 'forced labor' is the word for hard service or a term of duty, and her iniquity 'has been pardoned' translates a verb from the root ratsah, which commonly means to accept or be pleased with. It is the very verb of Leviticus 26, where the land 'enjoys' its sabbaths and where Israel 'pays the penalty' for iniquity, Leviticus 26:34, 41 and 43. Isaiah takes the language of exile's accounting and says the account has been accepted as settled.

The word 'double' is kiflayim, a dual form from a root for folding over. It pictures something folded in two, a full measure, the meaning that the debate above weighs.

In verse 4, 'the uneven ground' is the Hebrew word for what is crooked or steep, the same root as the 'deceitful' heart of Jeremiah 17:9. The Greek version of Isaiah, used by Luke, makes it 'the crooked ways shall become straight,' and the Gospel quotation carries a moral note along with a physical one. The contrasting 'plain' means level ground. The highway of verse 3 is a built-up road, a word related to the verb for heaping up or raising a roadway, as in 'build up the highway,' Isaiah 62:10.

Verse 6 is a puzzle in translation. The BSB says 'all its glory,' but the Hebrew word is chasdo, from chesed, the word usually rendered loyal love or loving devotion. Here it describes the faithfulness or charm of mortal people, and it fades like a flower. The Septuagint translates it as 'glory,' doxa, and Peter's quotation follows that, 1 Peter 1:24. God's chesed endures; the human version of it passes.

Verses 7 and 13 share a word. In verse 7 the grass withers 'when the breath of the LORD blows on them,' and in verse 13 the question is 'Who has directed the Spirit of the LORD?' The Hebrew word in both is ruach. The same ruach that withers the powers of the world is the one no counselor can instruct.

In verse 17 the nations are 'nothingness and emptiness,' and the second word is tohu, the very word of Genesis 1:2, 'formless and void.' The nations are as if the creation had never been brought out of chaos. The princes are brought to tohu in verse 23 as well.

In verse 18, the Hebrew for 'image' is demut, 'likeness,' the word God uses of humankind in Genesis 1:26. The question 'To what likeness will you compare Him?' therefore has a sharp edge: the only likeness God has made of Himself is a living human being, and no craftsman can cast another.

Finally, in verse 31 'renew' is the verb chalaf, which means to change or exchange. Those who wait on the LORD swap their weakness for His strength. In Isaiah 41:1 the nations are told to 'renew their strength' with the same verb, and the reader can hear the contrast.

typology.type: The voice and the highway, verses 3 to 5
typology.fulfillment: A herald calls for a road to be built for the LORD's arrival, with valleys raised and mountains made low. The Gospels apply this to John the Baptist: 'This is he who was spoken of through the prophet Isaiah,' Matthew 3:3, and John himself says, 'I am a voice,' John 1:23. Zechariah, John's father, says that John will 'go on before the Lord to prepare the way for Him,' Luke 1:76. Isaiah's highway for the exiles' return becomes the road along which God Himself arrives in Christ, and the levelling becomes repentance, 'a baptism of repentance,' Mark 1:4. The type falls short in that John prepares the way but is not the one who comes, Matthew 3:11.

typology.type: The Shepherd who gathers lambs, verse 11
typology.fulfillment: The God who 'gathers the lambs in His arms' is the shepherd of Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34:11 and 12, where the LORD Himself searches for His scattered flock. Jesus claims the role: 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep,' John 10:11, and He puts the lost sheep on His shoulders, Luke 15:5. Hebrews calls Him 'that great Shepherd of the sheep,' Hebrews 13:20, and Peter calls Him the Chief Shepherd, 1 Peter 5:4. The type is exceeded at the cost: the Shepherd of Isaiah carries lambs, and the Shepherd of the Gospel carries them by dying.

typology.type: The word that stands forever, verses 6 to 8
typology.fulfillment: Isaiah sets the withering grass of human flesh against the word of God that stands. Peter hears the word as the gospel, 'this is the word that was proclaimed to you,' 1 Peter 1:25. John goes further: 'the Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us,' John 1:14. The Old Testament does not say that the word of verse 8 is a person, so this is a pattern to read with care, but the New Testament makes the line: the eternal Word entered the grass-like frailty of flesh and died, and rose, and 'stands forever.' The type falls short because Isaiah's contrast keeps word and flesh apart; in Christ they are joined.

typology.type: The herald and 'Here is your God!', verse 9
typology.fulfillment: The herald is to cry from a mountain, 'Here is your God!' The gospel word, euangelizo in Greek, is the one the Septuagint uses for 'bring good news' here and in Isaiah 52:7, and Paul quotes the second text for those who carry the message of Christ, Romans 10:15. Jesus begins His public ministry with 'the kingdom of God is near. Repent and believe in the gospel!' Mark 1:15. And John the Baptist points to Him with 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29, which is Isaiah's 'Here is your God!' fulfilled in a finger pointing at a man. The type falls short in that the herald announces the coming, while the Gospels announce the arrival.

study.christ:
Isaiah 40 reaches Christ by promise, by a person, and by a title.

It reaches Him by promise because it is where the New Testament begins its story. Mark opens his Gospel with this chapter, 'the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ,' Mark 1:1 to 3, and every Gospel makes John the Baptist the voice of verse 3. When Luke tells us that Simeon was 'waiting for the consolation of Israel,' Luke 2:25, the word consolation belongs to the same Greek family as the verb the Septuagint uses for Isaiah's command to comfort. Simeon takes the child in his arms and finds in Him what Isaiah promised.

It reaches Him by a person, because the phrase in verse 9, 'Here is your God!', is said of someone who is coming. The herald is told what to announce, and it is not an idea or a policy but a presence. The Gospels' answer is Jesus. John the Baptist points at Him and says, 'Look, the Lamb of God,' John 1:29. Verse 10, 'His reward is with Him,' finds its echo when Christ says, 'Behold, I am coming soon, and My reward is with Me,' Revelation 22:12. And verse 3 says 'our God.' The highway is for the LORD, and the New Testament lets the road lead to a man, not around Him.

It reaches Him as Shepherd. The One whom Isaiah describes as shepherding His flock, gathering lambs and gently leading the nursing ewes, is the God of Ezekiel 34, who says, 'I Myself will search for My flock.' Jesus speaks in that voice, 'I am the good shepherd,' John 10:11, and then does what Isaiah could not yet say: He lays down His life for the sheep. The picture of a God strong enough to rule is joined to a Shepherd willing to die.

It reaches Him as Creator and Word. Verses 12 to 26 declare that the LORD alone made and holds all things. John says of the Word that 'through Him all things were made,' John 1:3, and Paul says that 'in Him all things hold together,' Colossians 1:16 and 17. Hebrews says the Son is 'upholding all things by His powerful word,' Hebrews 1:3. What Isaiah says of the LORD, the New Testament says of Christ, and it does so without any sense of having changed the subject.

The chapter also asks what to do with a God who never grows weary, and the Gospels answer in a small phrase: 'Jesus, weary from His journey, sat down by the well,' John 4:6. The God who is not tired took on flesh that could be. He carried the weariness that Isaiah describes, and He says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest,' Matthew 11:28.

Not every phrase in the chapter is a veiled reference to Christ. The measuring of the waters and the grasshoppers are teaching about God's greatness, not about a coming person. The links hold where the New Testament makes them.
study.god:
Isaiah 40 gives one of the fullest portraits of God in the Old Testament, and what stands out is how many different things it holds together.

He is incomparable. The questions of verses 12 to 14 are impossible for anyone else to answer. No one measured the waters, no one weighed the hills, no one served as His counselor or taught Him justice. The nations, which seem to dominate the world, are a drop in a bucket and a speck of dust on the scales. The largest forests of Lebanon could not supply fuel and sacrifice enough to honor Him. The point is not that nations do not matter but that God does not depend on them, Acts 17:25.

He is Creator and Lord of history. He sits above 'the circle of the earth,' stretches out the heavens like a curtain, and brings princes to nothing. The same hand that spreads the heavens also decides how long a ruler lasts. For the exiles, this was the answer to the claim that Babylon had defeated Him.

He is all-knowing and attentive, and He names the stars. 'He leads forth the starry host by number; He calls each one by name,' verse 26. The one who knows each star by name is not likely to lose track of Jacob. This is why the people's charge, 'My way is hidden from the LORD,' is met with the question, 'Do you not know?' in verse 28.

He is everlasting and unwearied. 'The everlasting God, the Creator of the ends of the earth... will not grow tired or weary; His understanding is beyond searching out.' The Psalms say it another way: 'the Protector of Israel will neither slumber nor sleep,' Psalm 121:4. His strength is not a store that runs low. That is why He is the source of strength for others.

He is tender. The Lord GOD 'comes with might,' verse 10, and in the next verse, 'He tends His flock like a shepherd.' The might and the gentleness are not alternatives. The arm that 'establishes His rule' is the same arm that gathers the lambs. He adjusts His pace to those who have young, leading the nursing ewes gently.

He is holy. The only time He speaks in the long argument is verse 25, and He speaks as 'the Holy One.' Isaiah 6:3, 'Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Hosts,' stands behind it. His incomparability is not mere size but a different kind of being.

The chapter also hints at the doctrine of the Trinity from within the Old Testament. 'The word of our God' in verse 8 and 'the Spirit of the LORD' in verse 13 are both spoken of as belonging to the LORD yet in a way that invites thought, and later revelation fills in the details.

For worship, the chapter gives us reasons to praise and reasons to hope. We worship the God who has no equal, and we bring Him our weakness without embarrassment. He says to the weary what no idol can say. 'Lift up your eyes on high,' verse 26, is both a command to look and a reminder that He has not looked away.

crossReferences.note: The covenant warning that the exile fulfils: the land will 'enjoy its Sabbaths' while Israel is in the land of its enemies and Israel will 'pay the penalty for their iniquity,' and yet God says, 'I will remember My covenant.' Isaiah 40:2 is the other end of this passage, saying that the penalty has been paid and the account settled.

The LORD reminds Israel of the exodus: 'I carried you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself.' Isaiah 40:31 uses the eagle's wings for those who wait on the LORD. The first deliverance becomes the pattern for the new one, and the image shifts from what God did to what He will do again.

'How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of those who bring good news... who say to Zion, "Your God reigns!"' It is the fulfilment of the herald's task in 40:9. What was an assignment in chapter 40 becomes an event, and Paul quotes it for the preaching of the gospel in Romans 10:15.

Luke gives the longest New Testament use of the passage, carrying the quotation all the way through the lifted valleys and lowered hills to 'all humanity will see God's salvation.' It makes plain that verse 5, 'all humanity together will see it,' is understood to reach beyond Israel.

Simeon is 'waiting for the consolation of Israel.' It belongs to the same family of words as the comfort of Isaiah 40:1, and Luke places it at the very start of his Gospel. It shows that devout Israelites read the book of Isaiah's comfort as something still ahead of them.

Peter quotes verses 6 to 8 and adds, 'And this is the word that was proclaimed to you.' The grass and the standing word are applied to the gospel preached to the churches, and their new life is therefore tied to the one thing that does not wither.

The LORD says, 'I Myself will search for My flock,' and promises to rescue the scattered, bind up the broken and strengthen the weak. It develops the shepherd of verse 11 and makes clear that this is a promise of God's own personal care, after the failure of Israel's human shepherds.

Paul closes his argument about God's wisdom with a quotation from Isaiah 40:13, 'Who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been His counselor?' He is saying that Isaiah's incomparable God is the God of the gospel, whose ways cannot be traced and who owes nothing to anyone.

The psalm joins Isaiah's two halves in three lines: God 'heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds,' 'determines the number of the stars; He calls them each by name,' and 'His understanding has no limit.' It is a commentary on verses 26 and 28 and shows how the nearness and the greatness of God belong together.

Moses' prayer uses the same grass: 'in the morning it springs up new, but by evening it fades and withers.' It places human frailty against a God who is 'from everlasting to everlasting,' Psalm 90:2. The two passages share one lesson, that mortality is the right background for trusting God.

Paul tells the Athenians that the God who made the world is not served by human hands 'as if He needed anything,' and that we should not think 'the Divine Being is like gold or silver or stone.' It is Isaiah 40:12 to 20 spoken in a Greek city, to people with idols of their own.

Jesus says, 'I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep.' He takes up the role of verse 11 and adds what the verse does not say: the Shepherd's care will cost Him His life.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's first poem about the world, Genesis 1, says that God spoke and the heavens were made. Isaiah 40 asks the exiles to look up at the same heavens and remember who made them. The Lord who spread the stars as a curtain is the God who called Abraham outside to count them, Genesis 15:5, and who now calls them each by name. The chapter is in this sense a return to creation: when everything seems lost, Isaiah goes back to the beginning.

It also answers the story of the fall. The curse of Genesis 3 brought human flesh to dust, and Isaiah calls humanity 'grass.' But the same chapter that says 'the people are grass' says that the word of God stands forever, and that is the thread that carries the story. God's promises do not wither with those who received them.

The larger story it belongs to is the exile and return. Israel's deliverance from Egypt was the shape of redemption, and the prophets promise a second exodus: a road through the wilderness, the LORD leading His people like a flock, water in the desert, Isaiah 35 and 43. Chapter 40 is where that promise begins to be spoken aloud. It was partly answered when Cyrus's decree sent exiles home, Ezra 1:1, but Isaiah's own language, 'all humanity together will see it,' pointed beyond that.

The New Testament says that the real answer came with Jesus. John the Baptist is the voice in the wilderness, and Jesus is the Shepherd and the Lord whose glory is revealed, John 1:14. Sin, the root of the exile, is dealt with, 'Look, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world,' John 1:29. Yet the promise of Isaiah 40 still has things left to do. People still grow weary, rulers still look permanent, and the exile of the world from God's presence is not yet over.

The new creation is where the chapter ends. Revelation 21:3 and 4 says that 'God Himself will be with them as their God,' and that He will 'wipe away every tear.' Revelation 7:17 describes the Lamb as the shepherd who leads His people to springs of living water. The grass of Isaiah 40 will not fade there, because the word of God that stands forever will have done what it was sent to do, and the waiting that Isaiah described will turn to sight.

sermon.title: Behold Your God!
sermon.why: Begg's four part series walks straight through Isaiah 40:1-31, the whole passage covered in this study, showing how God urges His people to respond to national calamity by casting their eyes afresh on Him as gentle Shepherd and holy, transcendent King.

quiz.q: What command opens this chapter in verses 1 to 2?

options.text: Comfort My people, for Jerusalem's iniquity has been pardoned.
options.note: Verses 1 to 2 give exactly this command, marking the turn from judgment to comfort.

options.text: Judge My people more severely for their sins.
options.note: The opposite; the command is to comfort, since the punishment is declared complete.

options.text: Warn My people of even greater coming judgment.
options.note: Not the content of these verses, which announce pardon and comfort, not further warning.

options.text: Ignore My people until they repent further.
options.note: The opposite; God commands His messengers to speak tenderly, not to withhold comfort.

quiz.q: How do the Gospels apply the voice crying in the wilderness, verses 3 to 5?

options.text: To John the Baptist, who prepared the way for Jesus.
options.note: All four Gospels apply this passage directly to John the Baptist's ministry.

options.text: To the prophet Isaiah himself and no one else.
options.note: The Gospels apply it specifically to John the Baptist preparing the way for Christ, not to Isaiah's own ministry.

options.text: To a future angelic being with no human identity.
options.note: The Gospels identify a specific human figure, John the Baptist, not an angelic being.

options.text: To the Babylonian officials who allowed the exiles to return.
options.note: The New Testament's application is to John the Baptist and Christ, not to Babylonian officials.

quiz.q: What contrast does verses 6 to 8 draw between human life and God's word?

options.text: All flesh is like grass that withers, but the word of God stands forever.
options.note: Verses 6 to 8 state this contrast directly.

options.text: Both human life and God's word are equally temporary.
options.note: The opposite; the passage contrasts fleeting human life with God's enduring, permanent word.

options.text: Human life is eternal while God's word changes over time.
options.note: The passage reverses this: human life withers like grass, while God's word alone endures forever.

options.text: Only the wicked wither like grass, not the righteous.
options.note: The text applies this to 'all flesh' generally, not selectively to the wicked alone.

quiz.q: What image describes God's incomparable power in verse 12?

options.text: He has measured the waters in the hollow of His hand and weighed the mountains on a scale.
options.note: Verse 12 uses exactly this image of effortless, immense power.

options.text: He struggles to control the seas and mountains.
options.note: The opposite; the image conveys effortless mastery, not struggle.

options.text: He shares equal power with the sun and moon.
options.note: The passage presents God as uniquely incomparable, not sharing power with created things.

options.text: He created the earth but has since withdrawn from governing it.
options.note: The passage presents God as actively measuring and governing creation, not withdrawn from it.

quiz.q: What promise closes the chapter in verse 31?

options.text: Those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles.
options.note: Verse 31 gives exactly this climactic promise of renewed strength for those who wait on God.

options.text: Only young, strong people will ever find renewed strength.
options.note: The opposite; the passage specifically contrasts even tired youths with those who wait on the LORD, who alone are renewed regardless of natural strength.

options.text: Waiting on the LORD guarantees the removal of all future hardship.
options.note: The promise concerns renewed strength and endurance, not the total absence of future hardship.

options.text: Strength comes only through human effort and training.
options.note: The opposite; the chapter contrasts human effort, which grows weary, with strength that comes specifically from waiting on the LORD.

questions: God's comfort begins by declaring that Jerusalem's sin has been dealt with. Where do you need to receive that same comfort, believing your sin is truly pardoned in Christ rather than still held against you?
John the Baptist prepared a straight highway for the LORD's coming. What obstacles, valleys, or crooked places in your own heart need to be leveled to make room for Christ this season?

All flesh is like grass, but God's word stands forever. What are you currently trusting in that is more fragile than you realize, and how could you anchor yourself more in God's enduring word instead?

God is pictured as both the Creator who measures oceans in His hand and the Shepherd who carries lambs close to His heart. Which of these truths, His greatness or His tenderness, do you need to remember most today?

The chapter promises that those who wait on the LORD will renew their strength. Where are you currently running on empty, and what would it look like this week to actually wait on Him rather than push forward in your own strength?

translationNotes.note: Double for all her sins is best understood as a Hebrew idiom for full, complete measure rather than a literal doubling of just punishment; the point is that Jerusalem's time of discipline is fully finished.
All four Gospels quote this verse and apply it to John the Baptist, Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4-6, John 1:23, making it one of the most directly cited verses from Isaiah in the New Testament.
Wait renders the Hebrew qavah, which carries the sense of eager, hopeful expectation rather than passive delay, closer to straining forward in hope than simply marking time.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched via the makor-scripture tool for Isaiah 40:1-31.
